# River Landscapes

- **Source** – The start of a river
- **Drainage Basin** – an area of land drained by a river and its tributaries
- **Tributary** – a small stream that joins a large river
- **Confluence** – where one river joins another
- **Mouth** – Something Alfie uses too mu- I mean where the river meets the sea
- **Watershed** – the line that separates one drainage basin from another

## River Cross Profiles

In the upper course, the river flows in a V shape. This is because there is not much water that is drained into the river, so there is less energy in the river, so the river cannot erode laterally (left/right) only vertically (down), causing it to form a V shape.
In the middle course the sides of the river start to erode, as the drainage basin area is larger, meaning more water drains into there river here, so the river has more energy. This makes it possible for the river to erode both laterally and vertically, so it starts to erode the sides.
In the lower course of the river, the sides have completely eroded. This is because the drainage basin area is now very large, so the river has a lot of water and therefore energy, so it can erode vertically and laterally a lot, causing both sides to erode and also making the river very deep.

## Bradshaw Model

![](data:image/png;base64,)

That is the Bradshaw model. Basically, it shows how different river characteristics change as you go downstream. Discharge is how much water passes a point in a second. Everything else is self-explanatory, except for like load quantity which is just the total mass of all the things that the river is carrying, and ig load particle size, which is the average size of something the river is carrying. Slope angle is the steepness of the sides of the river.
As you go down a river, a few things happen:
- The amount of water that gets drained into the river increases (drainage basin size increases)
- This gives the river more energy
- So, it can erode more (sides of the river)
- AND it can carry heavier objects
- Those heavy objects hit each other to become smaller
- It also causes the water to move faster

## River Erosion

Attrition – Where rocks hit each other or roll over each other and go from large, jagged and rough to small, rounded and smooth.
Abrasion – Where rocks scrape the riverbanks and bed and erode it
Hydraulic power – The force of the river water on the riverbanks and bed
Solution – where the river water can dissolve rocks in a chemical reaction, most commonly limestone, so the river can flow underground.

## Transportation In Rivers

Traction – Upper course – Large, Jagged and rough rocks roll in a circular motion in the direction of the current. They roll since the river has very little water and therefore very little energy to carry or the rocks, making them slowly roll instead.
Saltation – Middle Course – Smaller, more rounded but still large rocks are briefly kept up by the river, before falling back down to the riverbed, then bouncing back up again and being suspended for a few seconds, before falling again. This happens as the river has more water and therefore more energy than in the upper course, also the rocks are smaller and therefore easier to carry since they have been eroded, however the river does not have enough energy to fully keep the rocks afloat, so they fall after a few seconds.
Suspension – Lower Course – Very small and fine sediment is carried in the river and doesn’t fall. This happens because the lower course has the most water and therefore the most energy, and the material has been eroded fully now, so it is very light and easy to carry by the river.
Solution – Dissolved rocks flow in the direction of the current. Happened in all 3 courses since they are very light and the river has enough energy to keep them afloat.

## River Landforms Created By Erosion

Deposition – where the river drops materials being carried
Larger sediment is deposited first since it is heavier and needs more energy to be carried, so it is deposited before the more fine sediment.
WATERFALLS – Waterfalls are formed when there is hard rock over soft rock. The water flows over the hard rock and then over the soft rock, which then erodes through hydraulic power and abrasion. Eventually, the soft rock erodes around the hard rock, forming an overhang of the hard rock. This overhang eventually gets undercut enough so it collapses, which causes the rocks from the collapsed overhang to erode the soft rock under it (abrasion) and the force of the falling water (hydraulic power) also erodes it. This creates a plunge pool. The soft rock keeps getting eroded under the hard rock, causing more overhangs and the cycle repeats as the river retreats (mis hairline) backwards. A steep sided gorge forms where the river dips (waterfall)
Happens in the upper course. Also, you need to know a waterfall example, the one we were taught is called High Force Waterfall (refer to this in an exam if asked), but I personally think this one looks better:

## River Landforms Created By Erosion And Deposition

MEANDERS – Now it doesn’t actually say in my book how these guys form but I remember watching a video about it so enjoy my scuffed explanation:
One way a meander can form is if an animal like a fox burrows near a river channel. The soil where that burrow is is weaker than the surrounding soil, so the river (hydraulic power) erodes it faster, causing it to collapse (fox becomes homeless). The river now flows slightly towards the old burrow, and since the water is travelling fastest on the side closer to the burrow (this will be explained later), the side closer to the old burrow erodes faster and causes the river to begin to bend. The other side of the river begins to deposit sediment as the river water is traveling slower here since it has less energy, so it deposits sediment and forms a slip-off slope, which eventually forms new land.
The river is deepest on the outside of the meander since the water is traveling faster, so it has more energy, so it can erode vertically faster, making it deeper.
The water on the outside of the meander flows the fastest since it experiences the least friction from the riverbed and the air, since it is the furthest from the bed or the air, making it flow faster.
The eroded material is deposited on the inside of the meander since the water is traveling slowest (closer to channel bed and air) so it has less energy, so the river cannot carry the materials and instead deposits them, forming a slip-off slope, which eventually forms new land.
OXBOW LAKES - The river meanders, and on the outside of the river there is erosion, and on the inside of the river there is deposition. This causes the river neck to become thinner. Deposition and erosion continue, until the river neck is now very thin and both channels are very close to each other. During a flood event, the river can burst through the neck and flow in a straight line through to the other side. Some water still flows through the old meander. Deposition occurs at the start and end of the old meander, (energy deposition the drill) So eventually the old meander is completely cut off from the river, forming an Oxbow lake.

## River Landforms Created By Deposition

FLOODPLAINS – The river flows normally. When the river floods, it bursts it’s banks and floods the surround area, causing it to lose speed which causes it to lose energy, making it deposit sediment in the flooded area. Heavier, larger sediment is deposited first, next to the river, as it requires more energy to carry, while smaller, more fine sediment is deposited furthest from the river as it requires the least amount of energy to carry. After the flood, the river returns to normal flow, and the deposited sediment remains in the originally flooded area, causing a raised, fertile floodplain to form.
ESTUARIES – Where the river meets the sea. The river slows down, causing it to deposit sediment
